title: Solar Battery Degradation: What to Expect Over 10+ Years
excerpt: All home batteries lose capacity over time — here's how fast it actually happens, what affects it, and how to slow it down.
body:
Battery storage is a significant investment — most Australians spend between $8,000 and $15,000 on a home system. So it's worth understanding what happens to that battery over the decade-plus you plan to own it, rather than discovering it mid-way through.

## What Is Battery Degradation?

Degradation simply means a battery holds less usable energy than it did when new. A battery that shipped with 10 kWh of usable capacity might hold only 7–8 kWh after several years of daily cycling. The electricity still flows — you just get fewer hours of backup or export before it empties.

This is a normal electrochemical process, not a fault. Every lithium battery — in your phone, your EV, or your solar system — degrades. The question is how fast.

## Typical Degradation Rates for Home Batteries

Most lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries — which dominate the Australian home market — degrade more slowly than the older NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) chemistry. Here's what manufacturers and real-world data suggest:

| Chemistry | Typical warranty end-of-life capacity | Expected real-world lifespan |
|-----------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------|
| LFP (e.g. BYD, Powerwall 3) | 70–80% of original | 10–15+ years |
| NMC (older units) | 60–70% of original | 8–12 years |

Manufacturers express warranties in cycles *or* years — whichever comes first. A 6,000-cycle warranty on a battery cycled once daily equals roughly 16 years. But if your battery cycles twice daily (common with time-of-use tariffs), that halves the warranted cycle life to about 8 years.

Read your warranty document closely. Capacity guarantees and defect guarantees are different clauses.

## What Speeds Up Degradation?

Several factors within your control influence how quickly your battery ages:

- **High operating temperatures.** Heat is the primary enemy of lithium cells. A battery sitting in a western-facing garage in Brisbane summers will degrade faster than one in a cool, shaded location. If your installer proposes an unshaded outdoor spot in a hot climate, ask about an alternative.
- **Consistently charging to 100% and discharging to 0%.** Most systems let you set upper and lower charge limits. Keeping the battery between roughly 20% and 90% state of charge reduces stress significantly, at the cost of a little usable capacity each day.
- **High charge/discharge rates.** Pulling or pushing power very quickly (e.g. running a large ducted air con system entirely from battery) stresses cells more than steady, moderate loads.
- **Frequent deep cycles.** The deeper you regularly discharge, the faster cells age. Shallow, partial cycles are gentler.

## What You Can't Control

Some degradation is simply calendar ageing — cells change chemically over time regardless of how carefully you use them. This is why warranties expire by years as well as cycles. Even a battery that's barely been used for five years will have aged to some degree.

Australian summers also push ambient temperatures higher than most European battery test standards account for. If your area regularly sees 35°C+ days, factor that into your expectations.

## Practical Steps to Slow Degradation

1. **Choose the installation location carefully.** Indoors, in a laundry, garage, or under a staircase — anywhere shaded and ventilated — beats a hot north or west-facing external wall.
2. **Set charge limits in your inverter or battery app.** Many systems (Sungrow, SolarEdge, Enphase, BYD) allow you to cap maximum charge at 90% and set a minimum reserve of 15–20%. Check your app or ask your installer to configure this.
3. **Enable "self-consumption" or "time-of-use" mode** rather than forcing the battery to fully charge every day without need.
4. **Keep firmware updated.** Battery management system (BMS) software updates sometimes include improved charging algorithms that extend cell life.
5. **Get a performance check every 3–4 years.** A good solar installer can run a capacity test and compare it against your warranty baseline. Catching a genuine fault early gives you time to claim.

## When Degradation Becomes a Problem

If your battery drops below the warranted end-of-life threshold (usually 70–80%) within the warranty period, you have a valid warranty claim. Document your system's behaviour — most monitoring apps log daily charge/discharge history, and that data supports your case.

After the warranty period, you have choices: continue using a degraded battery (it still works, just with less capacity), replace just the cells if the inverter is compatible, or upgrade to a newer system.

## Actionable Takeaway

Check your battery's warranty document this week and note two things: the capacity guarantee percentage and the cycle or year limit. Then look at your monitoring app and calculate roughly how many cycles per day you're averaging. That tells you whether cycles or years will be your binding constraint — and whether your current usage habits are on track to maximise the life of your investment.
